name: Wendy Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Marsh Lane Produce, which grows carrots, onions and cabbages for one of the big supermarkets, about seven hundred acres of flat black soil, with some winter barley in the rotation and a few beef cattle on the grass margins. I'm in my second year. My day's on the cabbage side: checking crops, walking the rows for pests, helping the harvest gang, and then a lot of time on the tablet logging what's ready for which order.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace. When the supermarket wants an order in by Thursday, everyone pulls together, and when we make it, there's this tired, proud feeling in the yard. What wears me out is that I'm still not great with my hands. Eddie, the harvest foreman, can trim a cabbage in two seconds, and I'm still taking five and getting told off.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use one to help plan the harvest rota, one to spot pests from photos, and I've been reading everything I can about the weeding robots. I pushed Mr Garside, the owner, to trial one last spring, and it actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good, use it more, and I'd probably bore everyone at church with how the pest app saved a field of cabbages. Online I'd post about the weeding robot trial. I'm proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it makes me more useful than I'd be otherwise. I'm slow in the field, but I'm quick with the tools. That's my way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Mr Garside to buy the weeding robot properly, not just trial it. I'd do a short course in crop protection, so I know what I'm talking about with pests. And I'd keep saving, Mark and I have the cottage and about a year's money besides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit eager. Like the start of a good season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the cottage.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's on Church Lane, two up two down. My parents helped with the deposit and we've paid off most of the rest because Mark's a good mechanic and we don't go out much. It's ours, more or less, and it's why I'm not scared of much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope to be doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running my own farm, if God's willing. Maybe a hundred acres of veg, sold to the supermarket and a few local shops. I'd want to own the land, not rent it. My grandfather farmed in the old country and he always said, own the ground or you're just a guest.

S0.say: I'd say it's good and we should use it more, and I'd bore people at church with how the pest app saved a field of cabbages. I'd post about the weeding robot trial online because I'm proud of it.
S0.think: I think it makes me more useful than I'd be otherwise, because I'm slow in the field but quick with the tools. That's my way in.
S0.do: Pushes Mr Garside to buy the weeding robot outright and takes a short crop protection course. Keeps saving with Mark on top of their almost-paid-off cottage.
S0.feel: Calm and eager, like the start of a good season.
S0.quote: My grandfather farmed in the old country and he always said, own the ground or you're just a guest.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is ambitious and quick with tech, and open about being slow in the field. Her security comes from an almost-paid-off cottage and a year of savings. Her dream of owning land, and her grandfather's saying, frame how she sees everything that follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if firms hire fewer beginners, it's up to families and churches to help young people find a way in, with apprenticeships, not benefits. I'd say farms should take on youngsters who are willing to learn. I'd say it to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'm already in, I'm good with the tools, and I'm the kind of beginner a farm would still want. But my cousin's boy, Daniel, wants to farm, and I'd worry for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Garside if Daniel can come for the summer harvest, and I'd teach him the tablet side myself. I'd keep pushing the weeding robot, because the farms that use these tools first will be the ones still hiring. And I'd keep saving towards my own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little worried for Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the farms that use the tools first will keep hiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'll make money, and farms that make money take on people. The ones that don't change will go under, and then nobody's hired. That's how the market works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say the tools are why beginners aren't hired. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they're half right. But the answer isn't to stop the tools. It's to make sure young people learn them, which is what I'd do with Daniel.

S1.say: I'd say if firms hire fewer beginners, families and churches should help young people in through apprenticeships, not benefits. Farms should take on willing youngsters.
S1.think: I'd be fine, because I'm in and good with the tools, the kind of beginner a farm still wants. I'd worry for my cousin's boy Daniel, who wants to farm.
S1.do: Asks Mr Garside to take Daniel on for the summer harvest and teaches him the tablet side herself. Keeps pushing the weeding robot and saving toward her own land.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little worried for Daniel.
S1.quote: The ones that don't change will go under, and then nobody's hired.
S1.fieldNote: Her free-market view is clear: farms that adopt tools first will survive and keep hiring. When challenged, she conceded the critics are half right but still wants young people taught the tools. She thinks in terms of family and church helping, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shake-up, and people need to retrain and move, not wait for the government. I'd say there are new jobs if people go and get them. I'd probably share stories of people who switched to farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for us. The supermarket's ordering, our paperwork, the harvest plan, an assistant could do all of that and I'd be the one running it. My worry would be Mark's sister, who does payroll at an office in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Garside to let me set up an assistant for the supermarket orders and the harvest plan, and to bump my pay if it works. I'd tell Mark's sister to come and see the farm, we're always short at harvest. And I'd put a bit more into savings, just in case the supermarket squeezes prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for me, a bit sorry for the office lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mark's sister actually come to the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate the first week. But she's tough, and the pay at harvest is good. I'd put her on the packing line with Eddie's wife, who'd look after her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. Should the government do anything at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep out of the way, mostly, and make it easy to start a business or take someone on. Maybe help with a course or two. But I don't want my taxes paying people not to work.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shake-up and people need to retrain and move rather than wait for the government. There are new jobs if people go and get them, and I'd share stories of people who switched to farming.
S2.think: I think it's good for us, because I'd be the one running an assistant for supermarket orders and harvest plans. My worry would be Mark's sister, who does payroll in town.
S2.do: Asks Mr Garside to let her set up an assistant for orders and harvest planning, with a pay rise if it works. Invites Mark's sister to work the harvest packing line and adds a little more to savings in case the supermarket squeezes prices.
S2.feel: Excited for herself, a bit sorry for office workers.
S2.quote: She'd hate the first week. But she's tough, and the pay at harvest is good.
S2.fieldNote: Wendy sees a gain for herself and is happy to say so. Her answer to job losses is personal help, like getting her sister-in-law a harvest job, rather than government support. She did allow that a course or two might be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people shouldn't fight over the gains, they should go and earn their share. But I'd also say it's wrong if only the very rich do well. I'd want the government to make it easier to start businesses, not take more tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Physical work's safe, Mark's a mechanic, so his is too, and the cottage would be worth more. But land prices would boom too, and that's my dream of owning a farm gone, or pushed back years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and not buy anything at boom prices, because I'd rather wait for the bust. I'd ask Mr Garside about a share in the farm, or a small plot to farm myself on the side. I'd help people at church who lose their jobs, maybe with harvest work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frustrated about the land, safe for us, and a bit worried about the mood in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Garside give you a share in the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, honestly. But he's sixty-four and his kids aren't interested. If I make myself the person who runs the robots and the orders, I'm the obvious one to take over one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the bust. Are you sure there'd be one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. Nobody is. But my dad always says booms end, and I'd rather be early than broke.

S3.say: I'd say people shouldn't fight over the gains but go and earn their share. It's wrong if only the very rich do well, so the government should make it easier to start businesses rather than raise taxes.
S3.think: I'd be fine, with physical work, a mechanic husband and a cottage worth more. But land prices would boom too, which pushes my dream of owning a farm back by years.
S3.do: Keeps saving and refuses to buy at boom prices, waiting for a fall. Asks Mr Garside about a share in the farm or a small plot of her own, and finds harvest work for people from church who lose their jobs.
S3.feel: Frustrated about land, safe at home and a bit worried about the mood in town.
S3.quote: If I make myself the person who runs the robots and the orders, I'm the obvious one to take over one day.
S3.fieldNote: The boom hurts her not through her job but through land prices and her dream of owning a farm. She has a long game: become indispensable to an owner without heirs. She admitted she doesn't know if prices would fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms are coming whether we like it or not, so let's be first. I'd say the farms that buy robots will survive, and the ones that don't won't. I'd also say we should look after the people who lose jobs, through churches and families, not just the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be pleased for the farm and scared for the people. Eddie's harvest gang is thirty people at peak, and a robot harvester for cabbages would cut that to five. I'd be one of the five, I think, because I'm the robot person, but I'd be watching my friends go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd go to Mr Garside with a plan to buy robots before the farm next door does. I'd sooner the farm buys the robot than the farm next door does. That's not cruel, that's just how you keep the gate open. Then I'd take every course I could on running and fixing them, and I'd push to keep Eddie on as foreman for the robots, because he knows the crops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Eddie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's the one who knows when a cabbage is ready, and the robot needs someone like that. He'd say I'm talking him into his own funeral. He might be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your own family this picture reaches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He works in a warehouse, and that's the one I lie awake about. He's fifty-six and he's never done anything else. If his job goes, Mark and I would have him and Mum to stay, and he could help on my plot if I ever get one.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms are coming whether we like it or not, so let's be first, because farms that buy them will survive. People who lose jobs should be looked after through churches and families, not just the government.
S4.think: I'd be pleased for the farm and scared for the people, since a cabbage harvester could cut thirty pickers to five. I'd likely be one of the five as the robot person, but I'd watch my friends go.
S4.do: Takes Mr Garside a plan in the first month to buy robots before the neighbouring farm does. Takes every course on running and fixing them, pushes to keep Eddie on as foreman for the robots, and offers her parents a home if her dad loses his warehouse job.
S4.feel: Excited and guilty at the same time.
S4.quote: I'd sooner the farm buys the robot than the farm next door does. That's not cruel, that's just how you keep the gate open.
S4.fieldNote: Wendy moves fast and without apology, but her guilt about Eddie's gang and her fear for her father were real. Her free-market logic is clear: be first or go under. Her dad's warehouse job was the one thing she said keeps her awake, and it came up only when I asked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one, mostly because of Dad and Eddie's gang. I'll be fine, but they won't. What would help is help for older people to move into new work without losing face, and making it easier for people like me to buy small bits of land, so the robots don't all end up on the big estates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people round here will get through whatever happens because of church and family. That's not in any of your pictures, but it's real.

headlineQuote: I'd sooner the farm buys the robot than the farm next door does. That's not cruel, that's just how you keep the gate open.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old junior on a vegetable farm supplying a supermarket, slow at trimming cabbages but quick with AI tools, which she uses daily, and the person who pushed the owner to trial a weeding robot. She and her husband Mark, a mechanic, have almost paid off a cottage and have about a year saved, and she dreams of owning her own land. Her views are traditional and free-market: be first or go under, and look after people through family and church rather than the state. She sees most pictures as chances for herself, the boom as a threat to her land dream, and in the robot picture she pushes hard to buy first while feeling guilty about Eddie's harvest gang and frightened for her father in his warehouse job.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because of her father in his warehouse job and the harvest gang who'd lose their work.
whatWouldHelp: Help for older workers to move into new work without losing face, and easier ways for people like her to buy small plots of land so robots don't all end up on big estates.
